fullText: In 1180 London, there was a public cook shop on the tempames that never closed. Not on Sundays, not on Christmas, not ever. It served every rank of person, nobles, sailors, beggars, apprentices. And it did that 900 years before Door Dash existed. This was medieval England's first fast food restaurant and its own contemporary chronicler could not quite believe it was there. His name was William Fitz Steven. He was a cler in the household of Thomas Beckett and around the year 1180 he wrote the first detailed description of London ever recorded. In it he described the tempside cook shop like this. There is a public eating house. Every day according to the season, you may find roast and boiled meat, fish large and small, coarser flesh for the poor, delicate for the rich, such as venison and small birds, every day according to the season, for every social class. Fitz Steven wrote it casually as if this was already old news by 1180. Which means the medieval fast food economy was already ancient when he picked up his quill. By the end of the next 20 minutes, you will understand what medieval England actually ate when it wanted junk food. You will see the meat pies so dangerous. London passed a law to ban what was inside them. You will meet the pretzel blessed by the Catholic Church. And you will hear the shopkeepers who were dragged through the streets with their own bad bread tied around their necks. And you will meet one boy who ate all of it. His name is Watt. 17 years old, apprentice mason at the rebuild of old St. Paul's Cathedral. And in his entire life, he has never once cooked a meal for himself. Watt is 17 years old and he is one of the reasons the medieval fast food economy existed. He works 6 days a week on the scaffolding of old St. Paul's Cathedral, the massive Norman rebuild that has been going on in the middle of London for a 100red years and will keep going for 100 more. His job is to haul stone. He wears a rough wool tunic, a leather belt, and a small canvas bag of tools. He earns 2 p a day. 2 p. That is enough to keep him alive barely. And here is what those two p cannot buy him. A kitchen. What sleeps in a shared upper floor room in a wooden tenement near Cheapside. He shares it with four other apprentices. There is no hearth. There is no cooking pot. There is no chimney above them. Chimneys in 1180 London were a luxury only wealthy households could afford. Fuel was expensive. Firewood, charcoal, and Pete all had to be hauled in from the countryside and sold by weight. A working boy like what could not afford it. And even if he could, he had no legal fire in his room to burn it in. His stomach knew this before his brain did. In 1180 London, the majority of workingclass residents could not cook at home. They physically had no way to do it, which meant that every single meal, every single day had to be bought hot from someone else's fire. That was the economy Fitz Steven was watching. That was why the cook shop on the tempames never closed. What wakes at dawn? His stomach is empty. His purse holds 2 p from yesterday. He steps out into the cold London morning. Temp street is already alive and the smell hits him from a 100 m away. Fresh. Cooks Row was not a street name we would find on a modern map. But in 1180 London, if you asked anyone where to eat, they would send you here. A short lane branching off bread street close enough to the tempames that boats unloading fish had a straight walk to the cauldrons. Fitz Steven names it in his description. And what Watt walks into is one of the most sensory streets in the medieval world. The first thing is the smoke. Every shop has a hearth burning openly. Some outside on the cobbles, some just inside the doorway. Vendors have deliberately positioned their grills at the street's edge. This is not a ventilation problem. This is marketing. The medieval cook shop learned early that the smell of hot fat and roasting meat did more for sales than any painted sign. Bristol cooks would later formalize the practice. Cooking on hearths on the pavement itself. Food you could smell from streets away. Then the sound. Wafer irons hissing shut on batter. The dull knock of pies dropping onto wooden boards. Sellers shouting prices. Cauldrons of pottage bubbling. Small roast birds, quail, sparrows, thrushes stacked in wooden trays by the dozen. Then the food. Meat pies in a heavy pastry shell. The medievals called it a coffin. Pasties folded into half circles. Fritters glazed with honey. Small round hot cakes that could be eaten in one bite. wafers pressed in iron molds and stamped with the crucifixion and pottages, thick stews ladled into hollowedout slabs of stale bread. The bread was the plate. When you finished the stew, you ate the plate. A hot pie cost roughly one penny, half of Watt's daily wage. But it was hot, it was filling, and it would last him until the sun was overhead. He hands over his coin. He gets his pie. And the meat inside it may have been sitting on that grill for 2 days already. The meat pie in Watt's hands is the medieval hamburger. Hot, portable, greasy, filling, the single most popular fast food item in medieval England. It is also the most dangerous thing he could put in his mouth. The pie's genius was its shell. Medieval bakers called the pastry casing a coffin, a rigid, thick, tomblike crust designed to seal the filling inside. In wealthy kitchens, the coffin was cracked open at the table so guests could eat the meat within, and the crust itself was often discarded. In cook shops, the crust was cheaper to make than the meat, and it did something no other food container could do at the time. It hid the smell of spoiled meat. In 1219, a report from Norwich documented cooks knowingly using diseased pork in their pies and serving them to customers without a second thought. It was not an isolated case. Two centuries later, in 1379, the city of London passed an ordinance that officially banned cook shops from reusing unsold pie meat after one day. Which means that until 1379, doing exactly that was legal, routine, and expected. By the late 14th century, the reputation was so bad that Jeffrey Chaucser put a real London cook into the Canterbury tales. His name was Roger of Wear. He is documented in London City Records as an active pie maker. In Chaucer's story, Roger has an open sore on his shin that he cannot stop scratching while he cooks. The other pilgrims tease him about the pies he sells. Everyone in Chaucer's audience laughed because they knew exactly which pie. There was a medieval saying that survived from this world. God sends the meat, but the devil sends the cooks. But the merchants selling this rotten food were not operating without consequences. When they got caught, medieval London had a very specific punishment waiting for them, one designed to be seen. Medieval London did not wait for the modern food inspector to arrive. It built its own version 600 years before the FDA existed, and it did not rely on paperwork. In 1266, King Henry III passed the A size of bread and ale, the earliest documented food safety regulation in English history. The law set standards for how much a loaf of bread should weigh at every given price of grain, and it prescribed a very specific punishment for bakers who cheated their customers. The baker caught selling an underweight loaf was tied to a horse or hurdle. His fraudulent bread was strung around his neck on a rope. And he was dragged through the streets of the city he had cheated. Every neighbor saw him. Every customer he had defrauded saw him. That was the point. Butchers caught selling rotten meat faced the pillary. A wooden frame that clamped a man's head and hands in place at the level of a passing crowd's fists. The spoiled meat was often hung from the frame beside his own face for hours. In 1364, London took the same principle further. A city ordinance ordered that any tavern caught watering his wine be forced to drink his own diluted product in public in front of the customers he had cheated until the container was empty. The people enforcing all of this were called the guild wardens. Trade members whose own reputations depended on the honesty of their industry. They walked the markets daily, checking weights, smelling meat, spot-checking bread against the asai table. The punishments were savage on purpose. In a medieval city, food fraud could spark actual riots because bread was not commerce. Bread was survival. But not every medieval junk food had a shady reputation. Some of them were blessed by the Pope. And one of them is still in every American baseball stadium tonight. The pretzel is 900 years old. A monk invented it and the Pope endorsed it. Somewhere in Europe, the exact origin is still debated between Italy, France, and southern Germany. A monk in the early Middle Ages took three ingredients and shaped them into a knot that would still be sold in every American baseball stadium a thousand years later. Water, flour, salt, three ingredients that any household or cook shop could produce in a shape that could be baked hard and stored for weeks. The medieval equivalent of a shelf stable snack. But what made the pretzel a Christian institution was the Catholic Church. During Lent, the 6-week fast leading up to Easter, meat, dairy, and eggs were forbidden for the entire faithful population of medieval Europe. 46 days of drastically limited eating. The pretzel, containing none of those forbidden foods, became the officially sanctioned snack of the Lenton season. Vendors sold them on Cook's Row alongside the same pies Watt was eating and the church put them to work. Medieval monks handed pretzels to children who could correctly recite their prayers. It is one of the earliest documented uses of food as an educational reward. Get the words right. Get the treat. The shape itself was symbolic. The three holes represented the Holy Trinity. The knotted arms represented a child folding her hands in prayer. The Latin word brechellle arms is the likely root of the pretzel's name. By 1180, the pretzel was in every fair, every church festival and every hand at Watts Church on a Sunday. But Lent did not just give medieval London the pretzel. It gave it an alcohol problem, the kind a Benedicting monk called out by name. Ale in medieval England was not a treat. It was survival. Small ale, a weak, watery beer with an alcohol content of about 1% was the daily beverage of every adult, every apprentice, and every child in medieval London. The reason was practical. Untreated water in a 12th century city was dangerous. It carried sewage, animal waste, and disease. Fermentation killed what was in it. Small ale did not get you drunk. It got you hydrated safely. An average adult drank close to a gallon of small ale every day. Children drank it from the age they could hold a cup. It was breakfast. It was lunch. It was dinner. What? carried a small leather flask of it on his belt to the scaffold. The stronger ales were saved for celebration and for the tavern. The ale houses of medieval London were the social heart of the city. Warmer than home, cheaper than firewood, where men and women drank together, gossiped, gambled at dice, made deals, and slept when they could not walk back to their tenementss. The 1266 a size that regulated bread also regulated ale because both were considered survival goods by the crown. And then there was Lent. Lent banned meat. It banned eggs. It banned dairy. It did not ban ale. In the year 1400, a Benedicting monk named Robert Ripen delivered a sermon calling this out by name. He accused the common people of getting more drunk during Lent than during the entire rest of the year because they had nothing else to consume. If you could not eat meat, you could still drink your calories. And the people of medieval London did exactly that for 6 weeks every spring. But there was one thing in medieval London that could make even the drunkest tavern patron stop and stare because it cost more than his monthly wage. The sugar you have in your kitchen right now would have bankrupted a medieval English laborer. In the 14th century, sugar's retail price in England ran between 1 and2 sterling per pound of sugar. A working man like what earning 2 p a day would have needed roughly 120 days of labor to buy a single pound of it. So it was not for him. Sugar sat on the tables of nobles and monasteries. It was used as medicine, as showpiece, as diplomatic gift. The famous subtleties at royal banquetss, elaborate edible sculptures of castles, dragons, and ships were built out of it and sometimes gilded with real gold leaf. For everyone else, there was honey. Honeybased fritters with the medieval doughut fried dough sometimes stuffed with ginger and almonds drizzled hot with honey and sold from cook shops at fairs at St. Bartholomew's fair in London held every August from the year 1133. Gingerbread was pressed into shapes of saints and knights and the wealthiest versions were gilded with real gold leaf. Funnel cakes were called crisps in medieval Europe. There were cuskinols, a real medieval English name for a real medieval snack. Sweet fruit filled ravioli boiled and then sugared. A medieval hostess pastry 700 years old. And there were waffles, which are older than you think. The Greeks were making waffles in the fifth century BC. They called them obelios. Medieval Catholic churches turned them into ecclesiastical wafers stamped with biblical scenes. The Dutch added the grid pattern in the 1400s. The waffle iron in your kitchen has a 2,500year-old design history. And here is the strangest thing about all of this. Medieval junk food did not die when the Middle Ages ended. It is on your plate right now. You just do not recognize it. Every medieval junk food we have talked about in this video is still being sold somewhere in the world right now. The pretzel your child eats at a baseball game is a direct descendant of the 12th century Catholic Lent snack. Same three ingredients, same knotted shape, same purpose. A shelf stable snack you can eat with one hand. The waffle you had for breakfast this morning traces back to ancient Greek ailios via the medieval Catholic wafer iron. The Dutch grid pattern added in the 15th century is now the standard on every waffle iron sold on earth. The fritter what could not quite afford in 1180 became the American doughut. Same fried honey sweetened dough. Same fair food format. The trencher, the hollowedout bread bowl, what scooped pottage from at Cook's Row is still served in San Francisco with clam chowder inside it. Panera bread built a national restaurant chain on the medieval trencher. The medieval meat pie became the Cornish pasti, the pot pie, the empanada, the samosa. Wherever hot food had to be carried, handheld, and eaten on the move, this design won. Gingerbread is still on the Christmas cookie tray. Unchanged in principle since it was pressed into saints at St. Bartholomew's fair in 1133. Funnel cakes still exist, still deep fried, still powdered with sugar, still sold from stalls at fairs. The stalls are just made of steel now. And the food truck, the icon of urban modernity, is Fitz Stevens 12th century tempside cook shop. Same economics, same physics, same customer. 900 years apart. So what does this actually tell us about the people who invented all of it? The sun is setting over Temp Street. What has finished his day on the scaffold at St. Paul's? 14 hours of hauling stone in November light. His shoulders ache. His hands are roar. The medieval English world that produced all of this was not a primitive backwater. The people who built it were early consumers, early food safety officials, early regulators. They faced the same problems we face. Cheap food against healthy food, convenience against safety, class access against community. They solved those problems with the tools they had. The distance between them and us is not intelligence. It is time.
